mainTopic: A מבוי ending into a רחבה or courtyard, and partitions that might change or fail
overview: The גמרא explains what רב and שמואל argue about regarding a מבוי that opens into a רחבה. Without a shared עירוב, they argue about an opening that looks closed from outside but open from inside (נראה מבחוץ ושוה מבפנים). With an עירוב, they argue about רב יוסף's rule that only a מבוי ending in the middle of the רחבה is permitted. רבה adds that the openings must not line up, and רב משרשיא adds that the רחבה must belong to many people, since a single owner may build on it. The source for this is a case brought before רבי: a מבוי closed by the sea and an אשפה, where he gave no ruling because those barriers might change. A private heap may be cleared away while a public one stays, and the same is true of a backyard. In practice, carrying in such a מבוי is forbidden. מרימר fenced סורא's alleys with nets, and רב חסדא rejected a loose mat as a לחי unless it is fastened with a peg. Finally, the גמרא examines רב's ruling about a מבוי breached into a courtyard and shows that it teaches something beyond the משנה and the ברייתא. That discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: What exactly is the argument in each case?
steps.stepSummary: Following its first assumption, that רב and שמואל disagree whether or not a shared עירוב was made, the גמרא asks what the point of argument is in each case.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to what we first thought, that they argue both when they made an עירוב together and when they did not: when they made an עירוב, what are they arguing about? And when they did not make an עירוב, what are they arguing about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to its first assumption and asks what exactly רב and שמואל disagree about in each of the two cases. This sets up the next two steps, which answer each case separately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases cannot be the same argument. With a shared עירוב, the people of the yard and the מבוי are allowed to carry between them, so that issue is gone. Without one, they are not. So the reason for the dispute must be different in each case, and the גמרא wants each reason spelled out.

keyTerms.meaning: According to what we first thought
They made an עירוב (a shared food arrangement that joins properties so people may carry between them on שבת)

steps.confusionAlert: This question is asked according to the גמרא's FIRST assumption (מעיקרא). Do not assume this is the final way the גמרא understands the dispute. It is working out what that first approach would mean.

phrases.english: And according to what first came into our minds

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין שֶׁעֵירְבוּ וּבֵין שֶׁלֹּא עֵירְבוּ פְּלִיגִי:
phrases.english: that they disagree both when they made an eiruv and when they did not make an eiruv:
when they made an eiruv, about what do they disagree?
When they did not make an eiruv, about what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the earlier assumption from the previous part of the sugya to define the dispute in each case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact point of disagreement between רב and שמואל in the case with a shared עירוב and in the case without one.

steps.title: Without an עירוב: the alley that looks closed from outside but open from inside
steps.stepSummary: Without a shared עירוב, רב and שמואל argue about a מבוי that looks closed when seen from the outside but looks even and open from the inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they did not make an עירוב, they disagree about a case that looks closed from the outside but is even from the inside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second half of the question from step 1: without an עירוב, the argument is about a מבוי that looks closed from one side and open from the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רחבה is wider than the מבוי. From inside the yard, the end of the מבוי looks like a doorway, so the מבוי seems closed. From inside the מבוי, the opening is even with its walls, so the מבוי seems to run straight out, like an open alley. The question is which view counts. If it counts as closed, carrying in the מבוי is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: It looks a certain way (closed) from the outside
It is even (flush) from the inside, so it looks open

steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of נראה מבחוץ ושוה מבפנים comes up many times in הלכות עירובין and מחיצות. It asks whether a partition or opening is judged by how it looks from outside or from inside.

phrases.english: Where they did not make an eiruv, they disagree
about something that appears [closed] from the outside and is even from the inside.
phrases.notes: From the yard, the opening looks like a doorway. From inside the alley, it is flush with the walls.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּשֶׁלֹּא עֵירְבוּ — פְּלִיגִי בְּנִרְאֶה מִבַּחוּץ וְשָׁוֶה מִבִּפְנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second half of the question in step 1, the case with no עירוב.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Without an עירוב, the dispute is whether a מבוי that looks closed from outside but open from inside counts as closed.

steps.title: With an עירוב: they argue about רב יוסף's rule
steps.stepSummary: With a shared עירוב, רב and שמואל argue about רב יוסף's rule: carrying is allowed only when the מבוי ends in the middle of the רחבה, not at its side.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they made an עירוב, they disagree about the rule of רב יוסף. As רב יוסף said: They only taught this when the מבוי ends into the middle of the רחבה. But if it ends at the side of the רחבה, carrying is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the other half of the question: with an עירוב, the argument is whether רב יוסף's rule is accepted. It then quotes that rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the מבוי opens into the middle of the wider yard, the yard's walls stick out on both sides. That makes the end of the מבוי look like a doorway, so the מבוי counts as closed. If it opens at the side of the yard, one wall of the מבוי runs straight into the yard's wall. Then the מבוי and yard look like one continuous strip, and carrying is forbidden. One of רב and שמואל accepts this distinction and the other does not.

keyTerms.meaning: They disagree (the matter they argue about)
They only taught this rule in the case of
A backyard or open area behind houses

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. In step 2 (no עירוב) the issue is how the opening looks from inside versus outside. Here (with an עירוב) the issue is WHERE along the yard the מבוי opens: the middle or the side.

phrases.english: Where they made an eiruv, they disagree about the rule of Rav Yosef.
For Rav Yosef said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁכָּלֶה לְאֶמְצַע רְחָבָה,
phrases.english: They only taught [the permission] where it ends into the middle of the backyard,
phrases.notes: The yard's walls stick out on both sides, so the alley looks closed

phrases.english: but if it ends at the sides of the backyard, it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: The alley's wall runs straight into the yard's wall, so they look like one open strip

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעֵירְבוּ — קָמִיפַּלְגִי בִּדְרַב יוֹסֵף. דְּאָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first half of the question in step 1, the case with an עירוב, and brings רב יוסף's rule as the point of dispute.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: With an עירוב, the dispute is whether to accept רב יוסף's rule that only a מבוי ending in the middle of a רחבה is permitted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף: a מבוי ending into the middle of a רחבה is permitted. One ending at the side of the רחבה is forbidden.

steps.title: רבה adds a limit: the openings must not line up
steps.stepSummary: רבה narrows רב יוסף's permission. Ending in the middle of the רחבה is allowed only if the opening from the מבוי into the yard is not directly across from the yard's opening to the public area.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: What you said, that ending into the middle of the רחבה is permitted, we only said when the openings are not across from each other. But if one is directly across from the other, carrying is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה builds on רב יוסף's rule and adds another condition for when carrying is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two openings: one from the מבוי into the yard, and one from the yard out to the רשות הרבים. If they line up, there is a straight path running right through, so the area looks open and carrying is forbidden. If they do not line up, the path is blocked by the yard's wall, so the permission of 'middle of the רחבה' still holds.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this in the case of
One directly across from the other

steps.whatToRemember: There are three layers. (1) Without an עירוב, the dispute is נראה מבחוץ ושוה מבפנים. (2) With an עירוב, the dispute is רב יוסף's rule: the middle of the רחבה is allowed, the side is not. (3) רבה adds that even in the middle, it is allowed only if the openings are not lined up across from each other.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
That which you said, "[ending into] the middle of the backyard is permitted,"

phrases.aramaic: לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא זֶה שֶׁלֹּא כְּנֶגֶד זֶה,
phrases.english: we only said it where one [opening] is not opposite the other,
phrases.notes: The alley-to-yard opening and the yard-to-public opening

phrases.english: but if one is opposite the other, it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: A straight path through makes the area look open

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: הָא דְּאָמְרַתְּ ״לְאֶמְצַע רְחָבָה מוּתָּר״, לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further condition to the permission in רב יוסף's rule from step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מבוי ending in the middle of a רחבה is permitted only when its opening is not directly across from the yard's opening to the public domain. If they line up, carrying is forbidden.

steps.title: Only a shared backyard qualifies, not a privately owned one
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא says that רבה's permission (openings not facing each other) applies only to a רחבה owned by many people. A רחבה owned by one person might later be built up, so carrying is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב משרשיא said: What you said, that when the openings are not across from each other carrying is allowed, applies only to a backyard owned by many people. But if the backyard belongs to one person, he might one day decide to build houses on it. Then the מבוי would be like one that ends at the side of the רחבה, and that is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רב משרשיא adds another condition on top of רבה's rule. The permission only works when the backyard belongs to many people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One owner can easily change his mind and build houses along part of the רחבה. That would leave the מבוי ending at the side of the yard instead of the middle, which רב יוסף's rule forbids. So we forbid carrying now, before the houses are even built. Many owners cannot easily agree to build, so their yard is stable.

keyTerms.meaning: A backyard owned by many people
A backyard owned by one person
At the sides of the backyard

steps.whyThisMatters: This introduces the idea of worrying about a future change in the physical setup. That idea drives the rest of this passage.

phrases.english: Rav Mesharshiya said:

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּאָמְרַתְּ ״זֶה שֶׁלֹּא כְּנֶגֶד זֶה מוּתָּר״,
phrases.english: That which you said, "if one is not opposite the other, it is permitted,"
phrases.notes: Refers to רבה's rule from step 4.

phrases.english: we said this only about a backyard belonging to many people,
but a backyard belonging to one individual,
sometimes he may change his mind about it
and build houses on it,
and it will become like an alleyway
that ends at the sides of the backyard, which is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows רבה's permission even further.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The permission applies only to a רחבה owned by many. A privately owned רחבה is forbidden, because the owner may build and change the layout.

steps.title: Where do we get the private-versus-public distinction?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source for treating a privately owned backyard differently from a public one.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do you say that we distinguish between a backyard of many people and a backyard of one person?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for רב משרשיא's distinction. This line sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not an attack. It asks for a precedent showing that חז״ל worry about future changes depending on who owns something. The answer comes right away in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do you say this?

phrases.english: And from where do you say

phrases.aramaic: דְּשָׁנֵי לַן בֵּין רְחָבָה דְרַבִּים לִרְחָבָה דְיָחִיד —
phrases.english: that we distinguish between a backyard of many and a backyard of an individual?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a source for step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that private and public ownership are treated differently when we worry about future changes.

steps.title: רבי gave no ruling on an alleyway closed by the sea and a garbage heap
steps.stepSummary: רבין בר רב אדא quotes רבי יצחק. A מבוי was closed by the sea on one end and an אשפה on the other, and רבי would neither permit nor forbid carrying in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבין בר רב אדא said in the name of רבי יצחק: There was a case of an alleyway whose one end ended at the sea and whose other end ended at a garbage heap. The case came before רבי, and he said neither that it was permitted nor that it was forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story as the source for the distinction. רבי refused to rule on a מבוי whose two ends were closed by natural barriers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story shows רבי unsure whether we can rely on barriers that might change. How this proves the private-versus-public distinction is not obvious yet. The גמרא first explains רבי's silence (step 8) and raises a challenge (step 9). Steps 10 and 11 then make the connection clear.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not expect the proof to be obvious yet. The link to private versus public ownership becomes clear only after the next challenge is resolved.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רָבִין בַּר רַב אַדָּא, אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: As Ravin bar Rav Adda said that Rabbi Yitzchak said:
There was an incident with a certain alleyway
whose one side ended at the sea
and whose other side ended at a garbage heap,
and the case came before Rabbi,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָמַר בָּהּ לֹא הֶיתֵּר וְלֹא אִיסּוּר.
phrases.english: and he said about it neither permission nor prohibition.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רָבִין בַּר רַב אַדָּא, אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּמָבוֹי אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 6 by bringing a precedent.
steps.raayaObject: The private-versus-public distinction of רב משרשיא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי's refusal to rule on a מבוי closed by the sea and an אשפה.

steps.title: Why רבי neither forbade nor permitted
steps.stepSummary: רבי did not forbid, because the walls exist right now. He did not permit, because the אשפה might be removed or the sea might build up a sandbank.
steps.simpleTranslation: He did not forbid it, because the walls are standing. He did not permit it, because we worry that the garbage heap might be taken away, and that the sea might pile up sand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains each half of רבי's silence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Right now the מבוי is properly closed, so there is no reason to forbid. But both barriers could change. Someone might clear away the אשפה, or a sandbank might form between the מבוי and the water. Either change would leave the מבוי open, so רבי would not give a permission.

phrases.english: He did not state a prohibition about it —
because the partitions are standing.
He did not state a permission about it —
we are concerned that perhaps the garbage heap will be removed,
and that the sea will throw up a sandbank.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רבי's silence in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The walls exist now, so there is no prohibition. They may disappear later, so there is no permission.

steps.title: Challenge: elsewhere we do not worry that a garbage heap will be removed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the worry about the אשפה. A משנה allows throwing onto a ten-טפחים garbage heap in the public domain on שבת, and there we do not worry that it will be removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But do we really worry that the garbage heap will be removed? We learned in a משנה: If a garbage heap in the public domain is ten handbreadths high, and there is a window above it, people may throw onto it on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reasoning given for רבי's silence. It cites a משנה where we clearly do not worry that an אשפה will be removed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ten-טפחים-high אשפה counts as a רשות היחיד. Throwing onto it from a window is moving from one private domain to another, which is allowed. If we worried that someone might clear part of it away and lower it below ten טפחים, this would be forbidden. So the two sources seem to contradict each other about the worry.

keyTerms.meaning: But we learned in a משנה
Ten handbreadths, the height that makes an area a private domain

phrases.english: But are we concerned that perhaps the garbage heap will be removed?
But we learned in a mishnah:
A garbage heap in the public domain
ten handbreadths high,
a window that is above it —
one may throw onto it on Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא תִּינָּטֵל אַשְׁפָּה? וְהָתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning given in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that we worry an אשפה will be removed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה lets people treat an אשפה in the public domain as a lasting רשות היחיד, so it does not worry about removal. That contradicts the worry used to explain רבי's silence.

steps.title: A public garbage heap differs from a private one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that we must distinguish between a public אשפה, which stays put, and a private אשפה, which may be cleared away.
steps.simpleTranslation: It turns out that there is a difference between a garbage heap of the public and a garbage heap of a private person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge from step 9. The משנה about throwing onto an אשפה in רשות הרבים speaks about a public heap, and nobody removes that. רבי's מבוי had a private heap, which its owner might remove.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that every אשפה is treated the same way. The answer is that ownership matters. A public heap is assumed to be permanent, but a private owner may decide to clear his own heap, so we worry about it.

keyTerms.meaning: It turns out / apparently (introduces an inference)
There is a difference / we distinguish
Belonging to the public / belonging to an individual

phrases.english: Apparently, there is a difference
phrases.notes: אלמא draws a conclusion from the contrast between the two cases.

phrases.english: between a garbage heap of the public
phrases.notes: The public heap stays where it is, as in the משנה about throwing.

phrases.english: and a garbage heap of an individual.
phrases.notes: A private heap may be cleared away by its owner, as in רבי's מבוי.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא שָׁנֵי בֵּין אַשְׁפָּה דְרַבִּים לְאַשְׁפָּה דְיָחִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 9 by showing that the משנה and רבי's case involve different kinds of heaps.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): public versus private ownership
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every אשפה is equally permanent, so רבי should not have worried that the heap would be removed.
steps.terutzMaskana: A public אשפה is presumed permanent, but a private אשפה may be removed, so the worry in רבי's case stands.

steps.title: The same distinction applies to a backyard
steps.stepSummary: The heap distinction becomes the source for רב משרשיא: a public רחבה differs from a private רחבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, there is a difference between a backyard of the public and a backyard of an individual.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the loop on the question of step 6. Just as a private heap may change, a private backyard may get built up. This supports רב משרשיא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 asked for a source showing that private and public ownership are treated differently. The heap case shows exactly that principle. Here it is applied to the רחבה: a single owner may build in his backyard, while many owners will not.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too (applies a principle to the current case)
Backyard / open courtyard area behind houses

steps.whatToRemember: Ownership affects permanence. Something owned by the public is assumed to stay as it is, while something owned by one person might be changed. That is why רבה's permission applies only to a public רחבה.

phrases.english: Here too, there is a difference
phrases.notes: Applies the heap principle back to רב משרשיא's case.

phrases.english: between a backyard of the public
phrases.notes: Nobody will build here, so it stays open.

phrases.english: and a backyard of an individual.
phrases.notes: The owner might build on it, so carrying is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא נָמֵי, שָׁנֵי בֵּין רְחָבָה דְרַבִּים לִרְחָבָה דְיָחִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the heap distinction from step 10 and uses it as the requested source for רב משרשיא's ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב משרשיא's distinction is supported: a private רחבה is treated as impermanent, just like a private אשפה.

steps.title: What did the Sages hold in רבי's case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the רבנן ruled in the מבוי case where רבי neither permitted nor forbade.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Rabbis, what did they hold?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. It is setting up the next step, which will report the ruling of the חכמים on the מבוי bounded by the sea and the אשפה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי stayed undecided, which suggests that his colleagues took a definite position. The גמרא wants to know what that position was.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis / the Sages (here: רבי's colleagues)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, what did they hold?
phrases.notes: Refers back to the case in step 7.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the heap discussion and returns to רבי's case to ask about the opposing view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The ruling of the חכמים about carrying in a מבוי closed off by the sea and an אשפה.

steps.title: First version: the חכמים forbid, and the הלכה follows them
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר אבדימי cites a ברייתא that the חכמים forbid carrying. רב נחמן rules that the הלכה follows the חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר אבדימי said: A ברייתא taught, 'And the Sages forbid.' רב נחמן said: The הלכה follows the words of the Sages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 12. The חכמים forbid carrying in that מבוי, and רב נחמן says that this is the practical הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים take the worry about the private heap and the sandbank seriously, so they forbid carrying outright. Because רב נחמן rules like them, carrying in such a מבוי is forbidden in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law follows the words of

phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Avdimi said,
it was taught: And the Sages forbid;
phrases.notes: A ברייתא recording the Sages' view on רבי's case.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
The halacha follows the words of the Sages.
phrases.notes: So carrying is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר אַבְדִּימִי, תָּנָא: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹסְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים forbid carrying, and the הלכה follows them, so carrying is forbidden.

steps.title: Second version: the חכמים permit, but the הלכה does not follow them
steps.stepSummary: An alternate version: the ברייתא says the חכמים permit, and רב נחמן says the הלכה is not like them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב יוסף בר אבדימי said, a ברייתא taught, 'And the Sages permit.' רב נחמן said: The הלכה does not follow the words of the Sages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second report of the same statements. In this version the חכמים are lenient, but רב נחמן rejects their view in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two versions disagree about what the חכמים held. Even so, in both versions רב נחמן's ruling leads to the same practical result: carrying in such a מבוי is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say (introduces an alternate version of a report)
The הלכה is not (like this view)

steps.whatToRemember: Whichever version is correct, the practical הלכה is the same: carrying in a מבוי closed by the sea and a private אשפה is forbidden.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the two versions lead to opposite rulings. They disagree only about what the חכמים said. In practice, both versions forbid carrying.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
phrases.notes: Introduces a different version of the same report.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Avdimi said,
it was taught: And the Sages permit;
phrases.notes: In this version the Sages are lenient.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
The halacha does not follow the words of the Sages.
phrases.notes: So carrying is still forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר אַבְדִּימִי, תָּנָא: וַחֲכָמִים מַתִּירִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternate version of step 13 with the Sages' opinion reversed, yet it reaches the same practical outcome.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים permit, but the הלכה does not follow them, so carrying is forbidden.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to both versions, carrying in this מבוי is forbidden in practice.

steps.title: מרימר blocks סורא's alleys with nets
steps.stepSummary: מרימר closed off the river-facing ends of סורא's alleys with nets. He did not rely on the riverbank, because sand might pile up and ruin it as a partition.
steps.simpleTranslation: מרימר blocked off the alleys of סורא with nets. He said: we are worried that the sea (or river) might raise up a sandbank.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports what מרימר actually did in סורא. He put up nets instead of relying on the riverbank as a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a steep riverbank could count as a partition closing off the alley. מרימר worried that sand would build up over time, making the bank low and no longer a real wall. So he put up nets as a dependable partition. This fits the theme of the earlier steps: a partition that might change or disappear cannot be relied on.

keyTerms.meaning: a bank of sand or silt that the water deposits

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a natural partition which can change on its own is not trusted for carrying on שבת.

phrases.english: Mareimar blocked off the alleys of Sura with nets.
phrases.notes: The alleys opened toward the river.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא יַעֲלֶה הַיָּם שִׂרְטוֹן.
phrases.english: He said: We are concerned that perhaps the sea will raise up a sandbank.
phrases.notes: If sand fills in, the bank is no longer a proper wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא brings a practical application of the second concern given for רבי's silence in step 8, that the sea may raise up a sandbank. מרימר applies it to the riverbanks of סורא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A riverbank is not relied on as a partition, because a sandbank may form. Nets are put up instead.

steps.title: A rolled mat placed at the bend of a crooked alley
steps.stepSummary: In סורא there was an L-shaped alley. The residents placed a rolled-up mat at the bend to act as a לחי.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain crooked alley in סורא. They rolled up a mat and set it at the bend of the alley.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא describes a case from סורא. This is a setup line, and the next step gives רב חסדא's reaction to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A crooked (L-shaped) alley raises the question of how to treat the bend. The residents tried to fix it cheaply by standing a rolled mat at the turn, as a kind of side post (לחי). The question is whether this is good enough.

phrases.english: There was a certain crooked alley in Sura;
they rolled up a mat and placed it at its bend.
phrases.notes: It was meant to act as a לחי (side post).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a second practical case from סורא about a weak partition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: This step only describes the case. The ruling comes in the next step.

steps.title: רב חסדא rejects the mat under both רב and שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says the mat works according to neither רב nor שמואל. רב requires a צורת הפתח, and שמואל requires a proper לחי, which a mat the wind blows over is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: This follows neither רב nor שמואל. רב says a crooked alley is treated like an alley open at both ends, so it needs a צורת הפתח. שמואל says it is treated like an alley closed at one end, but even then you need a proper לחי. This mat, which the wind blows over, counts as nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא rejects the residents' mat. He shows that it fails under both opinions about crooked alleys.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב treats the bend as if the alley were open on both sides (מפולש), so only a צורת הפתח (doorway frame) helps. שמואל treats it as closed on one side (סתום), so a לחי would be enough. But it must be a sturdy לחי. A loose mat that the wind knocks down is not a partition at all, so it fails even for שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: its law is like an alley open on both ends
a doorway frame: two posts with a beam across the top
its law is like an alley closed on one end

steps.confusionAlert: שמואל does not say any לחי is enough. He only lowers the requirement from a צורת הפתח to a לחי. The לחי itself still has to be solid.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: הָא לָא כְּרַב וְלָא כִּשְׁמוּאֵל.
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: This is neither like Rav nor like Shmuel.
According to Rav, who said its law is like an alley open at both ends,
it needs a doorway frame.
According to Shmuel, who said its law is like an alley closed at one end,
that applies only to a proper side post.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הַאי, כֵּיוָן דְּנָשֵׁיב בֵּיהּ זִיקָא
phrases.english: But this one, since the wind blows on it
and throws it over, it is nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This step rejects the practice described in step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: It rejects the rolled mat as a valid fix for the crooked alley under both opinions.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Under רב, a לחי is the wrong kind of fix. Under שמואל, the mat is not a stable לחי because the wind blows it over.

steps.title: A mat fastened with a peg does count
steps.stepSummary: If the mat is fastened to the wall with a peg, it is considered firmly attached and works as a לחי.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if someone drove a peg into it and fastened it, then it is fastened.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a small qualification to רב חסדא's rejection. It shows how the mat can be fixed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only problem with the mat was that it was unstable. Once a peg attaches it firmly, the wind can no longer knock it down. It then counts as a real לחי, at least according to שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: he attached it / it is attached

steps.whatToRemember: A partition must be stable. If it can easily blow away or be removed, it does not count. Once it is firmly fastened, it does count.

phrases.english: But if he drove a peg into it and attached it,
it is attached (and valid).
phrases.notes: It now works as a proper לחי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This step limits רב חסדא's rejection. It applies only to a loose mat.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the problem is only instability.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think a mat can never serve as a לחי.
steps.terutzMaskana: A mat fastened with a peg is a valid לחי.

steps.title: רב's ruling on an alley breached into a courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to examine רב ירמיה בר אבא's quote from רב. If an alley is breached along its full width into a courtyard, and the courtyard is breached on the opposite side, the courtyard is permitted and the alley is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the statement itself. רב ירמיה בר אבא said in the name of רב: If an alley was breached along its full width into a courtyard, and the courtyard was breached opposite it, the courtyard is permitted and the alley is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: With the word גופא, the גמרא goes back to a statement quoted earlier in the discussion so it can examine it on its own. This sets up the analysis that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The alley lost its entire back wall, so it now opens completely into the courtyard. The courtyard is wider, so it keeps pieces of wall on both sides of its breach and still counts as enclosed. That is why it stays permitted. The alley, open fully on its side, has nothing left to close it off, so it is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: 'the matter itself': returning to examine a statement quoted earlier

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the courtyard and the alley share the same result just because the same breach connects them. The courtyard keeps side walls around its opening, and the alley does not.

phrases.aramaic: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Returning to the matter itself: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba said in the name of Rav:
An alley that was breached along its full width into a courtyard,
and the courtyard was breached opposite it,
phrases.notes: The courtyard now opens to the public domain.

phrases.english: the courtyard is permitted, and the alley is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the practical cases, the גמרא goes back to a statement it quoted earlier.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If an alley is fully breached into a courtyard, and the courtyard is breached opposite it, the courtyard is permitted and the alley is forbidden.

steps.title: Isn't this already taught in our משנה?
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר עולא challenges רב's ruling as unnecessary. The משנה of a small courtyard breached into a big one seems to teach the same law.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר עולא said to רב ביבי בר אביי: My teacher, isn't this exactly our משנה? 'A small courtyard that was breached into a big courtyard: the big one is permitted and the small one is forbidden, because the breach is like a doorway of the big one.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר עולא asks why רב needed to say his ruling about the alley and courtyard. A משנה already seems to teach the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the small courtyard loses a whole wall, so carrying there is forbidden. The big courtyard still has wall on both sides of the gap, so the gap counts as a doorway and carrying stays permitted. The alley breached into a courtyard looks like the same case, so רב's statement seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't this our משנה? Used to argue that a statement teaches nothing new.
like its doorway (the gap counts as an opening, not a missing wall)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבָּה בַּר עוּלָּא לְרַב בִּיבִי בַּר אַבָּיֵי:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Ulla said to Rav Beivai bar Abaye:
My master, is this not our Mishnah?
"A small courtyard that was breached into a large one —
phrases.notes: The breach runs along the small courtyard's entire wall.

phrases.english: the large one is permitted and the small one is forbidden,
because it is like the entrance of the large one."
phrases.notes: For the big courtyard, the breach has wall remaining on both sides, so it acts like a doorway.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רב's ruling quoted in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the courtyard is permitted and the alley forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ruling seems to repeat an existing משנה, so saying it would be unnecessary.

steps.title: The משנה might apply only where the public doesn't walk through
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי answers that from the משנה alone we might limit the law to a courtyard without public traffic. רב teaches that even a courtyard the public passes through is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If I only had that source, I would have said: this applies only where the public does not walk through it. But where the public does walk through it, you might say that even the courtyard is forbidden too.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ביבי explains what רב's ruling adds beyond the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, nobody walks through the big courtyard on the way to anywhere. In רב's case, the courtyard opens to the alley on one side and to the street on the other, so people may cut through it. Without רב, we might think that traffic forbids carrying in the courtyard. רב teaches that it stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: If I only had that source, I would have said (introduces a mistaken first assumption)
many people tread through it (public foot traffic)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי מֵהָתָם הֲוָה אָמֵינָא:
phrases.english: He said to him: If from there, I would have said:

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּלָא קָא דָרְסִי בָּהּ רַבִּים,
phrases.english: this applies only where many people do not tread through it,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הֵיכָא דְּקָא דָרְסִי בַּהּ רַבִּים —
phrases.english: but where many people do tread through it —
phrases.notes: For example, the courtyard in רב's case, which opens to both the alley and the street.

phrases.english: say that even the courtyard is also forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20 by showing a difference between the cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (public traffic versus no public traffic)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Public traffic through the courtyard would forbid carrying there.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with public traffic, the courtyard is permitted. That is what רב's ruling adds.

steps.title: A ברייתא already says public traffic doesn't matter for שבת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא: a courtyard the public walks through is a public domain for טומאה but a private domain for שבת. So again, רב's ruling seems unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we also learned this: a courtyard that the public enters on one side and exits on the other side is a public domain for טומאה, and a private domain for שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 21. A ברייתא already teaches that public foot traffic does not ruin a courtyard's private status for שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For טומאה, a doubt in a public domain is ruled pure, so heavy traffic makes the courtyard count as public. For שבת, only the walls matter, and the courtyard stays a private domain even when people pass through. That is exactly the point step 21 claimed רב was adding.

keyTerms.meaning: But we also learned this already (challenges a claim of something new)

steps.confusionAlert: The same courtyard gets two different labels. It is public for טומאה (doubts are ruled pure) but private for שבת (carrying is allowed). Each area of law has its own definition of a domain.

phrases.english: But didn't we also learn this:
A courtyard which many people enter on this side
and exit on that side,
is a public domain regarding ritual impurity,
phrases.notes: So cases of doubt there are ruled pure.

phrases.english: and a private domain regarding Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 21 by showing that its new point is already taught.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 21 that רב teaches that public traffic doesn't forbid the courtyard
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא already rules that public traffic doesn't change a walled courtyard's private status for שבת.

steps.title: The ברייתא might apply only when the openings aren't lined up
steps.stepSummary: From the ברייתא alone, we might think its rule applies only when the entrance and exit are not directly opposite each other. The answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: If I only had that source, I would have said: this applies only when the openings are not opposite each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of step 22 by limiting the ברייתא to a narrower case. It is setting up a contrast with openings that face each other, which the next lines will complete.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the entrance and exit are not lined up, people walking through have to turn, so the courtyard doesn't feel like a straight road. When they are directly opposite, the courtyard looks like a street running through, and we might call it public. רב's ruling covers even that case, so it still teaches something new.

keyTerms.meaning: one not directly opposite the other (openings that are not lined up)

phrases.english: If from there, I would have said:

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי מִילֵּי, זֶה שֶׁלֹּא כְּנֶגֶד זֶה.
phrases.english: this applies only when one is not opposite the other.
phrases.notes: The contrast case, openings directly opposite each other, continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22 by limiting the ברייתא to openings that are not aligned.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (openings aligned versus not aligned)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: When the openings face each other directly, the courtyard would count as public and carrying would be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב teaches that the courtyard is permitted even in that case. This is completed on the next amud.
